title: Synthesis and mastery
theme: Integration of all C1/C2 skills — mixed conditionals + inversion + clefts + hedging + idioms + literary craft + register fluidity + native pronunciation + pragmatic moves
goal: Student integrates every prior C1/C2 skill into open-ended communicative tasks — code-switching across registers, building extended arguments, narrating with literary craft, and speaking with native rhythm.
connects_to: End of curriculum. Closes Charlotte's structured progression at full native-equivalent fluency.

units.title: Mixed-register narrative
units.grammar_focus: Open narrative drawing on literary craft (M14), cleft sentences (M03), ellipsis (M17), and casual fillers (M21) within a single short passage
units.real_life_context: You tell a short personal story that breathes — literary where it should breathe, casual where it should land.

grammar.sentence: Which sentence uses both a cleft and a literary verb?
options: It was on a Tuesday in March that the call finally came.
The call came on a Tuesday in March.
On a Tuesday in March the call came.
The call, finally, came on a Tuesday in March.
grammar.answer: It was on a Tuesday in March that the call finally came.
grammar.explanation: It-cleft for emphasis ("It was on a Tuesday in March that..."), plus "finally" lending the sentence weight and patience. Combines M03 (clefts) and M14 (literary verb choice). C2 integration uses these moves together.

grammar.sentence: Which closing sentence works as a literary fragment?
options: Nothing else to say.
There was nothing else to say.
Nothing else needed saying.
There remained nothing to say.
grammar.answer: Nothing else to say.
grammar.explanation: Sentence fragment for emphasis — drawing on M14 (literary rhythm). After a long sentence, a fragment lands the moment. Both options work; the fragment ("Nothing else to say.") is sharper, the participle phrase ("Nothing else needed saying.") is more elegant.

grammar.sentence: Open the next sentence with a casual filler that fits the register: "I knew what was coming. _____, it still surprised me when it actually arrived."
grammar.hint: Casual filler that signals casual register
grammar.answer: I mean
grammar.explanation: Casual filler drawn from M21 — "I mean" / "you know" / "honestly". Marks the shift from observation to feeling. Native narrative often uses one such filler per paragraph, particularly at moments of emotional pivot.

grammar.sentence: Sentence too long and dense for narrative rhythm: "She had spent fifteen years working at the company and during that time she had built three teams, launched two products, and somehow managed to keep her sense of humour intact throughout every reorganisation and budget cut."
grammar.hint: Vary rhythm — long sentence + short follow-up or fragment
grammar.answer: She had spent fifteen years working at the company. Three teams. Two products. And somehow — somehow — she had kept her sense of humour intact through every reorganisation.
grammar.explanation: Long sentence + tricolon fragment + emphatic repetition. Drawn from M14 (rhythm) and M13 (tricolon). Native narrative breaks dense sentences for breath. The fragment "Three teams. Two products." emphasises the scale.

grammar.passage: It was on a Tuesday in March that the call finally came. I had been waiting six weeks, and — I mean, by then I had stopped expecting anything specific. Walking back from the kitchen with a coffee in my hand, I almost missed the ring. The voice on the other end was the one I had hoped for. Funny how the moment you stop waiting is exactly when the wait ends. Nothing else to say.
grammar.question: What literary technique closes the passage?
grammar.answer: a sentence fragment ("Nothing else to say.")
grammar.explanation: The passage integrates: it-cleft opener ("It was on a Tuesday in March that..."), participle clause ("Walking back from the kitchen..."), casual filler ("I mean"), pseudo-cleft reflection ("Funny how..."), fragment close ("Nothing else to say."). Five distinct C1/C2 moves in six sentences.

units.title: Argumentative essay opening
units.grammar_focus: Open an argument integrating inversion (M02), clefts (M03), academic register (M12), and argument structure (M13)
units.real_life_context: You write the opening paragraph of a persuasive essay or op-ed — academic register, structural devices for emphasis, careful claim-hedging.

grammar.sentence: Which opener combines inversion and an academic register?
options: Rarely has a single technology divided opinion as sharply as artificial intelligence has in the past decade.
AI has divided opinion in the past decade.
AI has, like, really divided opinion.
Lots of people disagree about AI.
grammar.answer: Rarely has a single technology divided opinion as sharply as artificial intelligence has in the past decade.
grammar.explanation: Fronted "Rarely" forces inversion ("has a single technology divided") — drawn from M02. Academic register throughout (no contractions, formal vocabulary) — drawn from M12. Combines two C2 moves in one sentence.

grammar.sentence: Which sentence opens with a cleft and a hedge?
options: It is widely believed that the technology will reshape work — though it could be argued that the reshaping has already begun.
The technology reshapes work. Maybe.
People believe the technology will change things.
Work is changing.
grammar.answer: It is widely believed that the technology will reshape work — though it could be argued that the reshaping has already begun.
grammar.explanation: Impersonal passive cleft ("It is widely believed that...") combined with a hedged impersonal opener ("it could be argued that..."). Drawn from M05 (passive), M03 (clefts), and M08 (hedging). C2 academic writing layers these.

grammar.sentence: Open with an inverted concession: "_____ has a single regulation produced such fierce debate as the proposed framework now before parliament."
grammar.answer: Rarely
grammar.explanation: Fronted negative frequency adverb triggers inversion — opener of choice for argumentative emphasis. "Rarely has..." opens with weight, signals importance. M02 inversion in argumentative service.

grammar.sentence: Argumentative opener too casual: "AI is a big deal. People disagree about it. Some say it'll ruin things, others say it'll save us. What do you think?"
grammar.hint: Rewrite for academic register with at least one structural device
grammar.answer: Rarely has a technology generated as polarised a debate as artificial intelligence has in the past decade. It is increasingly clear, however, that the question is not whether AI will reshape society but how — and on whose terms.
grammar.explanation: Casual opener → academic opener with inversion ("Rarely has..."), formal vocabulary ("polarised debate", "increasingly clear"), and clausal complexity. Reframed argument question ("not whether... but how... and on whose terms"). Heavy integration of M02, M03, M12, M13.

grammar.passage: Rarely has a single technology divided expert opinion as sharply as artificial intelligence has in the past decade. It is widely believed that AI will reshape the nature of work, though it could be argued that the reshaping has already begun. What is genuinely at stake is not whether change is coming, but how the gains will be distributed — and whose voices will shape that distribution. This essay argues for a third path: a regulatory framework that prioritises distributive justice over both reflexive enthusiasm and reflexive caution.
grammar.question: According to the opening, what is genuinely at stake?
grammar.answer: how the gains will be distributed (and whose voices will shape that distribution)
grammar.explanation: The opening integrates: inversion ("Rarely has..."), impersonal passive ("It is widely believed..."), hedged cleft ("it could be argued..."), pseudo-cleft reframe ("What is genuinely at stake is not... but..."), academic thesis statement. Five distinct C2 devices in five sentences. Op-ed opening grade.

listening_speaking.text: Rarely has a technology divided opinion so sharply.
It is widely believed that change is coming.
It could be argued that the change has already begun.
What is at stake is not whether but how.
This essay argues for a third path.

units.title: Diplomatic conversation
units.grammar_focus: Concession (M10) + hedging (M08) + register (M11) + pragmatic openers (M21) — disagree firmly while preserving the relationship
units.real_life_context: You deliver hard feedback or push back on a position without damaging the working relationship — diplomatic register sustained across a full exchange.

grammar.sentence: Most diplomatic refusal:
options: With respect, I'd see it differently — though I take your point about timeline.
You're wrong.
No, that's not right.
I disagree completely.
grammar.answer: With respect, I'd see it differently — though I take your point about timeline.
grammar.explanation: Three diplomatic moves in one sentence: "With respect" (formal hedge), "I'd / I would see it differently" (soft contrast), "I take your point about" (concession). Drawn from M08 (hedging) and M10 (concession markers). Disagreement without damage.

grammar.sentence: Which feedback opener is most face-saving?
options: Honestly — and I mean this constructively — I'd push back on one specific point.
You're completely wrong.
This is bad.
I don't like it.
grammar.answer: Honestly — and I mean this constructively — I'd push back on one specific point.
grammar.explanation: Pragmatic opener "Honestly" + intentional reassurance "I mean this constructively" + scoped pushback "on one specific point". Drawn from M21 (pragmatic openers) and M11 (register awareness). Preserves face while opening honest critique.

grammar.sentence: Diplomatic reframe of a strong position: "_____ that the proposal has merit — but the timing concerns are non-trivial."
grammar.answer: I can see
grammar.explanation: Three diplomatic openers, all from M10 (concession markers). Each grants ground before pivoting. "Granted, X — but Y" / "I can see X, but Y" / "It's / It is true that X — but Y". Diplomatic argument pivots on acknowledging the other side first.

grammar.sentence: Blunt feedback: "Your slides are bad and the message is confused."
grammar.hint: Rewrite diplomatically with at least three softening moves
grammar.answer: Honestly — and I mean this only because I want the deck to land well — I think the message could be tighter, and the slides might benefit from another pass. To be fair, the substance is all there; it's just buried.
grammar.explanation: Diplomatic rewrite uses: "Honestly" (M21), "I mean this only because" (intentional reassurance), "could be tighter / might benefit" (modal hedges M19), "To be fair" (M10 concession), positive framing ("the substance is all there"). Same critique, preserved relationship.

grammar.passage: She knew the only way the message would land was through the long route. 'I can see why you'd frame it that way — and to be fair, the data does support the topline argument. That said, the deeper question, it seems to me, is whether we're optimising for the right outcome. With respect, I'd push back on the framing of success here.' Three concessions before a single disagreement. The other person leaned in instead of away.
grammar.question: How many diplomatic devices does the speaker use before reaching the disagreement?
grammar.answer: at least three — 'I can see why', 'to be fair', 'that said', 'with respect' (4 if all counted)
grammar.explanation: Diplomatic disagreement requires layered concession. The speaker grants ground three or four times before pivoting — each acknowledgement keeps the listener engaged. By the time the disagreement arrives, the relationship is intact. Integrates M08, M10, M11, M21.

units.grammar_focus: Contractions + connected speech (M20) + tag questions + backchannels + fillers (M21) + conversions (M16) — sounding fully native in informal exchange
units.real_life_context: You have a casual conversation that flows without effort — contractions, fillers, tags, backchannels, all naturally present.

grammar.sentence: Most natural casual register:
options: I'm gonna grab a coffee — wanna come?
I am going to obtain coffee — would you like to accompany me?
I am going for coffee.
I'd like to fetch coffee.
grammar.answer: I'm gonna grab a coffee — wanna come?
grammar.explanation: Casual register integrates contractions ("I'm / I am"), reduced "going to" → "gonna", noun→verb conversion ("grab"), reduced "want to" → "wanna". All drawn from M16 (conversion) and M20 (pronunciation reductions). The other options sound formal, translated, or alien.

grammar.sentence: Most native conversational reply to "Are you free Saturday?":
options: Should be — what's up?
I am free on Saturday. May I ask why?
Yes.
I shall be free, I believe.
grammar.answer: Should be — what's up?
grammar.explanation: "Should be" — ellipsis-rich casual reply (drops "I"; "be" replaces full verb phrase). "What's / What is up?" — informal opener inviting continuation. Integrates M17 (ellipsis), M20 (contractions), M21 (informal opener). Native short-answer pattern.

grammar.sentence: Casual reply with tag: "We're meeting at the usual place, _____"
grammar.answer: aren't we
grammar.explanation: Tag question "aren't / are not we?" for soft confirmation. Drawn from M21. Or universal "right?" for casual register. Both work; "aren't / are not we?" is slightly more polished, "right?" slightly more casual.

grammar.sentence: Too formal for casual context: "I will see you on Saturday. Would you be inclined to arrive at noon?"
grammar.answer: I'll see you Saturday. Wanna meet at noon? (or: See you Saturday — noon work for you?)
grammar.explanation: Casual rewrite: "I'll / I will" (contraction), drop "on" before "Saturday" in casual register, "Wanna meet" (gonna/wanna conversion), question framed as "X work for you?" — short native pattern. Removes formal phrasing not needed in casual exchange.

grammar.passage: The conversation flowed. 'You been working late again?' 'Mm-hm. Should be done by Friday, though.' 'Want to grab a drink after, yeah?' 'I'd love to. Same place as last time?' 'Yeah, sounds good.' 'Cool — text me when you're heading out.' Six exchanges, twelve seconds, zero formality.
grammar.question: How many native conversational features can you spot?
grammar.answer: at least six — 'You been' (dropped 'have'), 'Mm-hm' (backchannel), 'Should be' (ellipsis), 'grab' (verb), 'yeah?' (tag), 'I'd love to' (ellipsis+contraction), 'sounds good' (ellipsis)
grammar.explanation: Tight casual exchange packed with native features: dropped auxiliary, backchannel, ellipsis, verb conversion, tag, contraction, set phrase. C2 conversational mastery looks like this — every utterance shaped by native instincts simultaneously.

units.title: Full synthesis
units.grammar_focus: Code-switching across registers in a single extended exchange — formal academic, diplomatic professional, casual personal — within one continuous conversation
units.real_life_context: Real life shifts registers every minute. You hold a conversation that moves from formal to casual to diplomatic, all within ten exchanges — and your English shifts with it, every time, without you thinking about it.

grammar.sentence: Register-appropriate response to "Could you summarise the findings?":
options: The findings suggest a strong correlation, though further study is warranted.
The stuff we found shows things are connected, kinda.
Yeah, things are related, basically.
Stuff is, like, linked.
grammar.answer: The findings suggest a strong correlation, though further study is warranted.
grammar.explanation: Formal/academic request → formal/academic answer. Modal hedge ("suggest"), passive ("is warranted"), hedged claim. Drawn from M12 (academic) and M19 (modal subtlety). Mismatched register reads as carelessness.

grammar.sentence: Register-appropriate reply to "We haven't seen each other in ages":
options: I know, right? It's been crazy.
Indeed. The intervening period has been considerable.
Yes. Time has elapsed.
It is correct that we have not met for an extended period.
grammar.answer: I know, right? It's been crazy.
grammar.explanation: Casual personal opener → casual personal reply. Contracted ("I know, right? It's / It is been"), informal vocabulary ("crazy"), tag question for warmth. Mismatching with formality would feel cold or robotic. Drawn from M11 (register) and M21 (casual register).

grammar.sentence: Diplomatic transition between casual and formal: "_____ — coming back to the actual decision in front of us..."
grammar.hint: Phrase that pivots from casual aside to substantive content
grammar.answer: Anyway
accepts: But to be serious for a moment
grammar.explanation: "Anyway" — universal pivot from digression back to topic. Casual register marker that doubles as a structural device. Drawn from M21. Native speakers code-switch within a single conversation, and "anyway" is one of the standard pivot points.

grammar.sentence: Same-register monotone across all turns: "Yes. Indeed. Yes. Indeed. Yes. The findings support that. Indeed. Yes."
grammar.hint: Vary registers — formal, casual, backchannels mixed
grammar.answer: Yes. Right — mm-hm. The findings do support that. Yeah. And, you know, the implications are pretty striking when you stack them up. Mm-hm, exactly.
grammar.explanation: Real conversation modulates: short backchannels ("Right — mm-hm"), substantive points ("The findings do support that"), informal connectors ("you know"), confirmations. Monotone replies sound like a chatbot. C2 fluency is rhythm + register variation.

grammar.passage: She moved through her morning at three registers. To the board, she wrote: 'It is recommended that the committee defer action pending a full review of the regulatory landscape.' To her co-founder, she texted: 'we need to push the board call to next week, the lawyers aren't ready.' To her best friend over coffee, she said: 'Honestly? The board's about to drive me up the wall — three months of this, and they still haven't read the brief.' Three registers, one truth underneath.
grammar.question: How does the speaker phrase the same underlying message to her best friend?
grammar.answer: 'Honestly? The board's about to drive me up the wall — three months of this, and they still haven't read the brief.'
grammar.explanation: Three registers, same content: formal board language ("It is recommended that..."), casual co-founder text ("we need to push..."), intimate friend chat ("Honestly? The board's about to drive me up the wall..."). C2 final mastery = effortless register switching, the right English for each room.
